subtype: Stage 1: A hurt that is not spoken [Actor]
passage: "You want to know why I've been weird all week? Fine." Kashish pulled her knees up on the bed. "Monday, lunch. Sachin and I have sat together since Class 6. Same bench by the basketball court. I came out with my tiffin, and he was sitting with the new kids from the quiz team, laughing. He didn't even look up. So I sat on the steps alone. Then on Tuesday he waved me over like nothing had happened, and I just... turned my face the other way. I couldn't ask him, 'Why did you leave me?' That sounds so needy. But I couldn't pretend it was fine either. So I say nothing. Every day. And it's killing me a little, Didi."

qa.q: Where have Kashish and Sachin sat together since Class 6?
qa.a: On the same bench by the basketball court.

qa.q: Why doesn't Kashish just ask Sachin what happened?
qa.a: She feels asking would sound needy, so pride keeps her quiet, yet she is too hurt to pretend things are fine. 😔

qa.q: What small step could stop this hurt from turning into a long silence?
qa.a: She could say one light, honest line to Sachin, like "I missed you at lunch on Monday", before the silence sets in.

qa.q: How might Sachin see Kashish turning her face away on Tuesday?
qa.a: Sachin may be confused, since he waved her over as if nothing had happened and likely doesn't know Monday hurt her.

grounding: Shows a teen girl who feels left out when her friend sits with others at lunch, too proud to ask and too hurt to act normal, so she goes quiet.

subtype: Stage 1: A hurt that is not spoken [Actor]
passage: I'm Yusuf. I sit at the table near the canteen window, so I see everything. Zainab and Abhinav always eat together, sharing her mum's parathas. Yesterday Abhinav walked in with the cricket lot and sat with them at the far table, laughing loudly. Zainab stopped in the doorway with her tray. For a second her face did something, like she'd been splashed with cold water. Then she sat down at the end of our table and opened a book. When Abhinav came past later and said, "Hey, you coming to the library?" she turned her face to the window and didn't answer. He stood there, then left. I don't know what she was thinking. But she read the same page for twenty minutes.

qa.q: Where did Abhinav sit yesterday?
qa.a: He sat with the cricket lot at the far table.

qa.q: What does Zainab reading the same page for twenty minutes suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she was hurt and distracted, not really reading, and didn't know how to act normal.

qa.q: What could Zainab do at this early stage instead of turning away?
qa.a: She could tell Abhinav simply, "I felt left out when you sat with them", which is small now but grows if left unsaid.

qa.q: How might Abhinav feel when Zainab turns to the window without answering?
qa.a: He is probably puzzled and a bit stung, standing there without knowing why she won't reply.

grounding: Shows, through a classmate's eyes, a girl hurt when her friend sits with others at lunch, who says nothing and turns away.

passage: In the study hall of the boarding school, Rashmi's phone lay face up beside her chemistry notes. Jatin's message had been sitting there since 7:40: "u ok? u left dinner early." She had read it eleven times. She wasn't going to answer. If she said what was wrong, that he'd laughed along when the others mocked her accent at dinner, he would probably say, "Relax, you're overreacting." Silence felt safer. Silence felt like the one thing she could control. Ramesh sir walked between the desks, checking that phones were away. Rashmi slid hers under her notebook but kept one corner visible, just in case it lit up again. Part of her wanted Jatin to keep trying. To notice. To come and find her.

qa.q: Since what time had Jatin's message been sitting there?
qa.a: It had been sitting there since 7:40.

qa.q: Why does Rashmi choose not to reply?
qa.a: She fears hearing "you're overreacting", so silence feels safer and gives her some control.

qa.q: What turning point is available to Rashmi now?
qa.a: She could reply briefly with the real reason, "The accent jokes at dinner hurt", rather than waiting for Jatin to guess.

qa.q: What is Jatin likely experiencing as his message goes unanswered?
qa.a: Jatin is probably unsure and uneasy, noticing something is wrong but not knowing what he did.

grounding: Shows a teen girl withholding a reply because silence feels safer than a fight, while hoping her friend will notice and come to her.

passage:
Dear Uday,
I'm not going to send this. That's kind of the point. You've texted me four times since Saturday's practice, and I've left every one on "seen". I know it's mean. But if I reply, I'll have to say that it hurt when you told Coach I wasn't ready for the relay, like I'm the weakest girl on the team, and you'll say I'm too sensitive, and then we'll fight, and I'll cry, and you'll win. Not replying means I don't lose. It's the only part of this I'm in charge of. And honestly? Some small, silly part of me hopes you'll keep texting. That you'll show up at my gate and say, "Pallavi, what's wrong?" Then I'd know you actually care.
Your friend (for now)

qa.q: How many times has Uday texted since Saturday's practice?
qa.a: Uday has texted four times since Saturday's practice.

qa.q: What does Pallavi secretly hope will happen?
qa.a: She hopes Uday will keep texting and even come to her gate asking what's wrong, which would prove Uday cares.

qa.q: What could Pallavi try instead of leaving every message on "seen"?
qa.a: She could send one honest line, "What you told Coach hurt me", and ask Uday to hear it without calling her sensitive.

qa.q: What might Uday be feeling after four unanswered texts?
qa.a: Uday may feel worried and shut out, unable to guess what went wrong, and might soon stop trying.

grounding: Shows a teen girl choosing silence as protection from a fight and from being called too sensitive, while hoping her friend will come to her.

subtype: Stage 3: Confusion for the one ignored [Receiver]
passage: Nikita sat behind the counter of her father's kirana shop in Nashik district, weighing out sugar without looking at the scale. Gautam hadn't spoken to her in four days. Not at the bus stand, not at tuition, not even when she held out her mango to share like always. What had she done? She went through it again. Was it the joke about his cycle? Did he hear she'd topped the test? Was he angry she didn't come to his cousin's wedding? Between customers she scrolled back through their chats, three months of them, searching for the message that broke something. Nothing. If he'd shouted at her, at least she'd know. This quiet was worse. Her stomach hurt all evening.

qa.q: How many days had it been since Gautam spoke to Nikita?
qa.a: Gautam hadn't spoken to her in four days.

qa.q: Why does the silence feel worse to Nikita than shouting would?
qa.a: With shouting she would at least know what she did; the silence leaves her guessing and anxious, with her stomach hurting.

qa.q: What could Nikita do next instead of searching old chats?
qa.a: She could ask Gautam gently and directly, "I feel like something's wrong between us. Will you tell me?"

qa.q: What would change if Gautam told Nikita what was bothering him?
qa.a: Nikita could stop guessing wildly; even an angry answer would give her something real to respond to.

grounding: Shows a teen girl who is being ignored by a friend, guessing wildly and rereading old chats, finding the silence harder than open anger.

subtype: Stage 3: Confusion for the one ignored [Receiver]
passage: Fatima had read the whole chat three times now, all the way back to September. Mateo used to send her twenty messages a day: memes, homework answers, blurry photos of his dog. Since Friday, nothing. At school in Lyon he walked past her locker as if it were a wall. She lay on her bed making lists in her head. Was it because she'd laughed at his haircut? Because she'd sat with Inès in maths? Because she hadn't liked his last post fast enough? Each guess made her chest tighter. She typed "did I do something?" and deleted it. Then typed it again. If he'd just yelled at her, she'd know what to fix. Instead she felt shut out of something she couldn't even see.

qa.q: What did Mateo use to send Fatima?
qa.a: He used to send her memes, homework answers and blurry photos of his dog.

qa.q: How does Fatima feel as she makes lists of possible reasons?
qa.a: Each guess makes her chest tighter; she feels anxious and shut out without knowing why. 😟

qa.q: What would help Fatima right now?
qa.a: Sending the "did I do something?" message, or asking Mateo quietly after class, would replace guessing with a real answer.

qa.q: Why might Mateo not realise how much his silence is hurting Fatima?
qa.a: From outside, walking past a locker looks small; Mateo can't see her rereading chats and lying on her bed with a tight chest.

grounding: Shows a teen girl who cannot tell what she did, rereading chats and guessing anxiously, as a friend's silence shuts her out.

passage: I'm Jyoti, Ankita's cousin, and we walk to school together, so I've seen this whole thing. It's been nine days since Ankita stopped talking to Megha. At first Megha kept coming up to her: in the corridor, at the gate, with notes, once with Ankita's favourite chikki. Ankita would look away, but I saw the tiny smile when Megha walked off. She liked being chased, I think. Now Megha has stopped trying as much, and Ankita keeps checking the gate anyway. Yesterday she ate lunch alone and said she preferred it. Last night she told me, "If I talk now, after nine days, it'll look so stupid." Then she stared at her phone till the screen went dark.

qa.q: What did Megha once bring Ankita?
qa.a: Megha once brought Ankita's favourite chikki.

qa.q: What does Ankita's tiny smile when Megha walked off suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she enjoyed being chased and wanted back, even while keeping up the silence.

qa.q: What turning point is still open to Ankita after nine days?
qa.a: She could send Megha a simple message, "I've been silly and I miss you, can we talk?", accepting a moment of embarrassment instead of weeks more.

qa.q: What might Megha be going through now that Megha has stopped trying so much?
qa.a: Megha may feel tired and rejected after days of notes and chikki with no reply, and may now be guarding against more hurt.

grounding: Shows, through a cousin's eyes, a teen whose silence has become a punishment she half enjoys, while loneliness and embarrassment grow each day.

passage:

Day 6: Avni had asked four more times. He still said nothing. At home he opened their chat, typed "you know what you did", and deleted it. The house felt very quiet. He missed her voice notes about cricket.
Day 11: Avni had stopped asking. Jomon sat alone at recess, rehearsing ways to break the silence. Every version sounded more ridiculous than the last. After eleven days, how do you just say hi?

passage:
Shankar,
I'm leaving this in your maths notebook because you haven't answered my messages for a week, and I don't want to add more pings. I'm not angry. I can tell something's wrong, and I really don't know what it is. Maybe I did something dumb at the match. Maybe it's not about me at all. Either way, I'd honestly rather hear it, even if it's bad, than keep guessing. You don't have to write a long reply. You can just write "Tuesday after school" and I'll be at the tea stall. I'll listen first. I promise not to argue. And if it's something you can't say yet, that's okay too. I'll still be around.
Still your friend,
Madhav

qa.q: Where did Madhav leave the letter?
qa.a: Madhav left it in Shankar's maths notebook.

qa.q: What does Madhav want Shankar to feel when reading the letter?
qa.a: Madhav wants Shankar to feel safe rather than accused, so that speaking up feels easier than staying silent.

qa.q: Which parts of the letter make it easier for Shankar to reply?

qa.q: How might Shankar feel finding this letter after a week of silence?
qa.a: Shankar may feel relieved and a little embarrassed, with an easy way back that doesn't require admitting fault. 🙂

grounding: Shows a teen gently naming a friend's silence without accusation and inviting the truth, making speaking safer than staying quiet.

passage: "So I didn't know what to do," Sarika said, sitting cross-legged on the terrace with her cousin. "Irawati had gone totally silent. Eight days. And my first draft was awful: 'If you have a problem with me, just say it instead of acting like a baby.' I almost sent it. Then I thought, what would I want to get if I were her? So I deleted it and wrote, 'I can tell you're upset, and I honestly don't know why. I'd rather hear it, even if it's something I did.' That's it. No blaming. She read it at eleven at night. Nothing. Then at 11:40 she wrote, 'It was the Holi photo.' And we talked till one."

qa.q: What did Irawati say it was about?
qa.a: She wrote, "It was the Holi photo."

qa.q: Why did Sarika delete the first draft?
qa.a: Sarika imagined receiving it in Irawati's place and realised the accusation would only push Irawati deeper into silence.

qa.q: What made the second message work?
qa.a: It named the upset without blaming, admitted not knowing, and invited the truth even if it was Sarika's fault.

qa.q: What might Irawati have felt in the forty minutes before she replied?
qa.a: She may have been torn between pride and relief, deciding whether it felt safe enough to speak.

grounding: Shows a teen replacing an accusing draft with a kind message that names the silence and invites the truth, which gets the friend talking.

passage:
Class teacher's note, Grade 9B, 18 August.
Nazia and Bidisha have sat apart for about three weeks; Bidisha has looked more and more withdrawn. Today, as Nazia had asked, I let them use the empty art room during free period. I stayed at my desk at the far end, marking. Bidisha spoke first, quietly: "I felt left out at lunch. When you started sitting with the drama group." Her hands were shaking. Nazia looked shocked. "I thought you were angry about my birthday! I only sat there because they needed help with lines. I missed you." Bidisha laughed and then cried a little. Both seemed relieved, I think, that it was so small. Walking out, Nazia said, "Three weeks, for that." Plan: nothing further needed. Will keep an eye out.

qa.q: Where did Nazia and Bidisha talk?
qa.a: They talked in the empty art room during free period.

qa.q: What does Bidisha's laugh and small cry suggest?
qa.a: It suggests relief that the real reason was so small, after three weeks of fearing something worse.

qa.q: What lesson might both take from this?
qa.a: Saying "I felt left out" early would have cost a minute, while the silence cost three weeks of distance.

qa.q: What had Nazia believed the problem was?
qa.a: Nazia thought Bidisha was angry about the birthday, and had been missing Bidisha all along.

grounding: Shows a teen finally naming the hurt of being left out at lunch and finding the answer far smaller than the fear.

passage:
Wednesday
I did it. After two weeks of stomach-ache silence, I finally told Ishita. We were waiting for the school bus, and I said, really fast, "I felt left out when you went to the mall with Pihu and didn't ask me." My face was burning. I was ready for her to say I was being clingy, or that she didn't want me there. Instead she just said, "Oh no, I thought you had dance class. I'm so sorry." That was it! Two weeks of imagining the worst, and the real answer took ten seconds. We shared her earphones all the way home. Note to self: next time, say it on day one, not day fourteen.
— Aditi

qa.q: What was Aditi afraid Ishita would say?

qa.a: Say it on day one, not day fourteen, because the real answer was small and the silence cost two weeks of worry.

qa.q: How might Ishita have felt hearing about the mall trip?
qa.a: Ishita was probably surprised and sorry, since she truly thought Aditi had dance class. 😊

grounding: Shows a teen speaking the real hurt of being left out, getting a reply much smaller than feared, and resolving to speak up earlier.

passage:
The fight with Vinita last Saturday started with my parents visiting for a month, but by the end it was about everything. She was crying, I was shouting, and then something in me just switched off. I remember standing by the fridge with my hands cold and my throat locked. Every sentence I started in my head sounded like it would make things worse. So I said nothing. Not that night, not at breakfast. She thought I was punishing her. I wasn't, not at first. I just didn't have a single word that felt safe. It was like being underwater while she shouted from the surface. I'm her husband, and I know that silence isn't good enough.
— Rafiq

qa.q: What did the fight with Vinita start with?
qa.a: It started with Rafiq's parents visiting for a month.

qa.q: Why did Rafiq go silent after the fight?
qa.a: He felt swamped, with cold hands and a locked throat, and every sentence he imagined seemed likely to make things worse.

qa.q: What could Rafiq say at this stage so his silence isn't misread?
qa.a: Even one line, like "I'm overwhelmed and can't talk yet, but I'm not punishing you", would help Vinita understand.

qa.q: How did Vinita read his silence?
qa.a: Vinita thought he was punishing her, since she couldn't see that he felt as if he were underwater.

grounding: Shows a husband flooded after a harsh fight who falls silent because he cannot find safe words, not at first to punish.

passage:
Counsellor's session note, first meeting: Vaibhav (25) and Indu (24).
Indu opened by describing Sunday's argument about money. As she spoke, Vaibhav's voice rose, then broke off mid-sentence. From then on he went still: eyes on the carpet, arms folded tightly, jaw working. When I asked what was happening for him, he shook his head and whispered, "I don't know what to say that won't make it worse." Indu said this is what happens at home: after a fight he goes silent for days, and it feels to her like a punishment. I noted that his breathing was fast and shallow; he looked more overwhelmed than angry. Plan: next session, work on how he can signal "I need a pause" before shutting down.

qa.q: What was Sunday's argument about?
qa.a: It was about money.

qa.q: What does Vaibhav's whisper reveal about his silence?
qa.a: It shows he can't find words that won't make things worse, so his silence comes from overwhelm rather than a wish to punish.

qa.q: What does the counsellor plan to work on next?
qa.a: How Vaibhav can signal "I need a pause" before he shuts down.

qa.q: How does Indu experience the days of silence at home?
qa.a: She says it feels like a punishment, because from her side she can't see the overwhelm behind it.

grounding: Shows a husband who goes silent when a conflict feels too intense, overwhelmed rather than intending to punish, as a counsellor observes.

passage:
Subject: something I haven't told anyone

Mohit bhai,
You asked last week why Shruti and I seem "so polite" now. Here's the honest answer. A year ago, when we fought, I discovered that if I just went quiet, the shouting stopped. It worked. So I kept doing it. Now it's automatic. She raises the rent, or her job, or my mother, and I say "hmm, let's see" and switch on the cricket. We never fight anymore. We also never finish anything. The rent, the job, the Diwali plans, they're all still sitting there, stacked up behind "please" and "thank you". I'm starting to think polite is just another word for stuck.
Your little brother,
Divyansh

qa.q: What does Divyansh switch on when Shruti raises an issue?
qa.a: He switches on the cricket.

qa.q: What is Divyansh starting to believe about their politeness?
qa.a: He is starting to believe that polite is just another word for stuck.

qa.q: What turning point is open to Divyansh now that he sees the habit?
qa.a: He could pick one stacked-up issue, like the rent, and tell Shruti he wants to finish that talk, with a pause allowed if it gets heated.

qa.q: How might Shruti experience the "hmm, let's see" replies?
qa.a: She may feel dismissed and lonely, raising real concerns that never get resolved.

grounding: Shows a husband whose silence, first used to stop shouting, has become an automatic response while unresolved issues pile up behind politeness.

passage: "You want the honest version?" Tenzin rubbed the back of his neck. "When Binita and I argue, I've learned the fastest way to stop it is to not answer. The first time I did it, two years ago, it felt like magic. She ran out of steam, the flat went quiet, and I thought, good, done. Now I do it without deciding to. She says something about my late nights, and my mouth just closes. We're very polite now. 'Tea?' 'Thanks.' But the late nights, her sister's loan, the move to Pune, none of it ever got settled. It's all sitting there behind the politeness, like boxes nobody unpacks." He laughed without humour. "I think I built a wall and called it peace."

passage:
"Irfan, please. Just tell me what's wrong."
Silence. He kept scrolling.
"Is it about Sunday? About my mother? Say something."
"It's fine."
"It's not fine! You haven't said a real sentence in four days." Pooja's voice cracked. "I'm standing right here. Do I even exist?"
He put the phone face down but didn't look up.
"When I was small, my father did this. Days of nothing. I promised myself I'd never live like that again." Tears ran down her face. "Please."
Nothing.
She wiped her cheeks, hard. "Fine. Two can play this." She picked up her pillow and went to the other room, and this time it was her door that shut.

passage:
Looking back at that month, I barely recognise myself. When Sohail stopped talking after our fight about moving cities, I tried everything. I asked gently. I made his favourite biryani. I wrote him a note. I cried at the dining table. My friend Bidisha said, "Give him time," but every quiet evening felt like being erased. I felt like a wife talking to a wall. I kept thinking of being eight, waiting for my mother to notice me after my brother was born. By the third week the hurt turned into something hard. I stopped asking. I stopped cooking for two. I was angry, and honestly it felt better than feeling invisible. That's when the house went completely silent.
— Nazia

qa.q: What did Nazia cook to reach Sohail?
qa.a: She made his favourite biryani.

qa.q: Why did Nazia's hurt turn into anger?
qa.a: Anger felt better than feeling invisible, a feeling that echoed waiting as a child for her mother to notice her.

qa.q: What might have helped at this stage, before both went cold?
qa.a: A clear word from Sohail that he needed time and would return, or a counsellor's help if the silence kept going, could have stopped the slide.

qa.q: What might Sohail have noticed when Nazia stopped asking and stopped cooking for two?
qa.a: He may have felt the change as a door closing, and the colder, quieter house could make reaching out even harder for him.

grounding: Shows a wife who tries everything against her husband's silence, feels invisible as old fears stir, and whose hurt hardens into anger.

passage:
Thursday, 11 pm.
Day twelve. Tenzin and I passed each other in the kitchen tonight like two polite flatmates, not like a husband and his wife. "Salt?" "Here." That was our whole conversation. Neither of us has mentioned the fight about his job offer in Delhi. I keep thinking he should be the one to bring it up, since he went silent first. I bet he's thinking I should, since I stopped talking too. So we wait. The house is so quiet I can hear the clock in the hall. What scares me is what happens if we do talk and it goes like last time: shouting, slammed doors. So I don't. And the gap between us gets a little wider every night.
— Nirmala

qa.q: What was their whole conversation in the kitchen?
qa.a: "Salt?" "Here." That was their whole conversation.

qa.q: What is Nirmala scared of that keeps her from raising the job offer?
qa.a: She fears that talking will go like last time, with shouting and slammed doors, so she stays quiet.

qa.q: What small step could break this freeze?
qa.a: One of them could name the stuck feeling without blame, like "I miss you, and I'm scared of fighting again", and agree on a pause rule.

qa.q: What might Tenzin be thinking during these twelve days?
qa.a: Nirmala guesses he is also waiting for her to move first, since she stopped talking too, so both are held by pride.

grounding: Shows a married couple both avoiding the subject in a quiet house, each waiting for the other, held by pride and fear of another bad fight.
